item.title: Tyson Bagent Week 4 QB Grade: Jets @ Bears Film Breakdown
item.description: A deeper look with @iamcogs at Tyson Bagent and the Chicago Bears’ dominant 23*12 win over the New York Jets!
item.content:encoded:
Well, Ben Johnson got us again.

After spending the entire week refusing to publicly name his starting quarterback, Johnson decided to take things one step further Sunday afternoon. Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent both trotted onto the field for Chicago’s first offensive snap, with Bagent split out wide while Keenum took the snap, handed the ball off and promptly headed to the sideline.

So, technically, both quarterbacks started.

Very funny, Ben.

From that point forward, though, this was Tyson Bagent’s offense.

With Caleb Williams missing his second consecutive game due to the hamstring injury suffered against Minnesota, Bagent stepped back into the lineup after clearing concussion protocol and was tasked with following up Case Keenum’s fantastic performance against Philadelphia.

The result?

Another Bears win, and somehow an even more dominant offensive performance.

Chicago defeated New York 23-12, but the final score doesn’t come remotely close to explaining what happened at Soldier Field.

The Bears outgained the Jets 492-157, picked up 34 first downs compared to New York’s seven and possessed the football for an absurd 42:45. Chicago ran 89 offensive plays.

The Jets ran 32.

According to Football Perspective, that 89-to-32 split was the second-most lopsided play differential in NFL history, trailing only Pittsburgh’s 90-to-28 advantage over the expansion Browns in 1999.

It gets better.

Chicago actually finished with more first downs than New York had offensive plays, something SumerSports noted hadn’t happened in an NFL game since 2016.

The Bears’ 34 first downs were also their most in a game since at least 1941, while their +335 advantage in total yardage was Chicago’s largest since a +343 performance against the St. Louis Cardinals in 1979.

Oh, and Tory Taylor never had to punt.

It was one of those afternoons where it felt like the Bears had the football for about three hours while the Jets occasionally stopped by to run a few plays.

A lot of that credit belongs to the running game. Kyle Monangai absolutely wore New York down, carrying the ball 30 times for 146 yards and two touchdowns, while Chicago finished with 232 yards on the ground. That allowed Johnson to keep Bagent in favorable situations throughout the afternoon and control the game without asking his backup quarterback to carry the offense.

But Bagent held up his end of the bargain.

He completed 25 of 34 attempts for a career-high 268 yards, finishing with no touchdowns, one interception and an 84.0 passer rating. Those numbers aren’t going to jump off the page, especially after what Keenum did against Philadelphia, but I thought Bagent looked noticeably more comfortable operating this offense than the quarterback I charted back in 2023.

If you’ve followed my work for a while, you know I haven’t exactly been shy about my concerns with Bagent.

The arm talent is limited. That’s not suddenly going to change. There are throws Williams can make within this offense that Bagent simply cannot, and we’ve seen how that can restrict the field when defenses begin squeezing the underneath areas.

But what has changed is how comfortable he looks operating within those limitations.

Bagent has always gotten the ball out quickly and avoided sacks well, but against New York there was more confidence in what he was seeing. He played within structure, got through the concepts more consistently (but did have a few plays he perhaps moved through those concepts a bit too quickly, overlooking open receivers down field) and generally gave his playmakers opportunities to do the work after the catch.

When the pocket was clean, he was about as efficient as you could ask for.

Next Gen Stats had Bagent completing 21 of 23 passes from a clean pocket for 202 yards, performing 17.3 percentage points above expectation. Under pressure, however, things changed dramatically. He completed just four of 11 attempts for 66 yards with the interception.

That split does a pretty good job of illustrating both sides of Bagent’s afternoon.

When Chicago kept him comfortable and the offense stayed on schedule, he distributed the football efficiently and helped sustain drive after drive. When New York forced him off his spot or sped up the picture, some of the limitations and questionable decisions began to surface.

And the afternoon certainly wasn’t flawless.

The official box score lists one interception, but there were a few other throws where Bagent flirted with danger, including turnovers that were erased by Jets penalties. The interception that did count came on a pass behind Colston Loveland over the middle, giving Minkah Fitzpatrick New York’s first interception since the final game of the 2024 season.

So we’re not walking away from this pretending Bagent suddenly turned into a different caliber of quarterback. What we can say is that he looked like a more developed version of the player we saw three years ago. That’s exactly what you want from a backup quarterback.

The Bears didn’t need Bagent to play hero ball. They needed him to run the offense, stay on schedule, avoid sacks and allow the talent around him to take over.

For most of Sunday afternoon, that’s exactly what he did. And for the second consecutive week, Ben Johnson showed just how adaptable this offense can be without Caleb Williams.

Keenum beat Philadelphia by operating like the veteran point guard we talked about last week, consistently anticipating windows and getting the football where the design told him to go. Bagent brought a little more mobility and a quicker trigger against New York, while Chicago leaned even harder on its rushing attack and controlled the football for nearly three quarters of the game.

Different quarterbacks. Different approaches. Same result. The Bears are 3-1, and three different quarterbacks have now led them to victories through the first four weeks of the season, something no NFL team had accomplished that early since the 1997 Jacksonville Jaguars.

Now let’s see what the numbers say about Bagent’s afternoon.

Benchmarks

Stat Formatting Key: This week we will be comparing Keenum’s week 3 start against Williams’ Season Totals and Averages.

(Season totals are underlined, Season Averages in Italics, and this week’s stats appear in regular text.)

C/A:36/55 (65.5%) | 18/27.5 (65.5%) | 24/34 70.6%

Yards:407 | 203.5 | 247

Touchdowns: 4 | 2 | 3

Turnovers: 1 | 0.5 | 0

QB at Fault Sacks:0 |0| 0

aDOT:7.7 | 6.1

Passer Rating: 92.0 | 110.8

True Passer Rating:113.4 | 122.0

Time to Throw:3.34s | 2.19s

Time to Pressure:2.75s | 2.27s

Pressure Rate:41.57% | 23.68%

On-Target Rate:83.3% | 63.6%

Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 7.5% PPR / 5.0% BRP | 0.0% PPR / 7.3% BRP

EPA per dropback:+0.31 | +0.18

ANY/A:6.2 | 8.4

Game Scorecard

The full grading sheet for each play can be found here.

Game Notes

Note: Last year, I included PFF grades in these breakdowns. With PFF continuing to expand its use of AI across its platform, and with my confidence in how accurately its grades reflect quarterback performance declining, I’ve decided to move away from them this season. In their place, I’ll be using PFN’s Impact Score, which will be notated as PFN on grading sheets moving forward.

  • NFL Passer Rating / True Passer Rating / PFN Impact Score: 83.9 / 102.5 / 80.8
    • The NFL’s average passer rating through Week 4 sits at 92.2, making Tyson’s 83.9 against the Jets very a below average start.
    • A 102.5 TPR hovers around the league average start mark of 100.0.
      • As a reminder, TPR has a built in checks and balances system when it comes to ADoT, Tyson’s ADoT was only 6.0 last week, dinging him slightly for overly cautious play.
    • On the PFN scale, where 75 represents an average qualifying starter and 90 is elite territory, Bagent finished Week 4 with a 80.8 Impact Score, ranking 7th of 32 qualifying quarterbacks.
      • Tyson’s strong EPA/db (+0.22), success rate (61.1%) and CPOE (+8.0%) really helped him crack the top 10 in impact score this week.
  • On-Target Throws: 2026 Average: 83.3% | Week 3: 73.3%
    • Reminder: Completion percentage ≠ On-Target Percentage. I only chart aimed passes, meaning throwaways, spikes and passes deflected at the line are excluded. Drops can still be credited as on-target.
    • Short-Level Passing (Behind LOS–9 yards): 17/22 | 77.3% On-Target
    • Deep-Level Passing (10–20+ yards): 5/8 | 62.5% On-Target
      • Overall Bagent was above league average when it came to on target throwing in week 4, he did have some rough misses that led to turnover worthy throws, however thanks to some timely flags those turnover don’t appear on the stat sheet. (the grading sheet, however..)
  • Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 11.6% PPR / 4.7% BPR
    • While a 11.6% poor play rate is less than ideal, Ben Johnson and Tyson Bagent watch and review the same tape I do, and know how to correct these areas of weakness much better than I could ever suggest.
  • Time to Throw:2.48 seconds
    • Tyson was overall quick with the ball, sometimes too quick, however. I counted at least 6 plays where Tyson either had a mad open downfield and did not throw to him, or moved off a deeper concept before it finished out, and dumped the ball off underneath. There is even an example on tape of this showing up in his and Burden’s body language, where Bagent moved off a concept for Luther Burden too quickly, and acknowledges it shortly after.
  • EPA per Dropback:+0.22
    • This mark ranked 11th among 32 qualifying quarterbacks in Week 4. So while Tyson accounted for exactly zero touchdowns directly, his EPA/db was better than Case Keenum’s week 3 mark by 0.04. A huge factor in that is the difference in success rate (Keenum: 51.4%, Bagent: 61.1%)
  • Under Pressure: 12.50%
    • The Bears offensive line dominated the Jets all afternoon, posting their lowest pressure rate allowed since week 17 of the 2025 season against the 49ers (17.39%).
  • The Bakery Open For Business?
    • I recorded three turnover worthy throws, and there were a total of five throws that were put into danger, two of which not getting a turnover worthy grade for the following reason:
      • An interception that came off Tyson realizing he had a free play and throwing deep.
      • An interception that came off a defensive player holding the intended receiver and sling-shotting ahead of him for the interception.
    • All three graded turnover worth plays came in the first half, and they all came in the “anticipation routes thrown late/behind” variety. A concern I’ve had with Tyson since his stint starting in 2023.

Play Reviews

The plays we’ll be reviewing are presented in the order they occurred in the game.

As a brief review, let’s recap the colors of the routes on these plays for those new to the process:

  • Blue: Indicates pre-snap motion or post-snap blocking.
  • Yellow: Routes other receivers run on the play.
  • Red: Route the targeted receiver runs.

Situation: 1st Quarter, 1st and 10 CHI47 11:38
Play Grade: Good
Result: 20-yard completion to Luther Burden III
Notes: (+) Anticipation (+) Mid-Level Accuracy/Completion (+) Explosive Play

Analysis: This is a nice example of Bagent throwing with anticipation over the middle. At the top of the screen, Burden pushes vertically before breaking inside on a deep dig, while Loveland runs a shorter in-breaking route underneath. Backside, Odunze runs a corner-post double move, selling the break toward the sideline before bending back inside.

What I really like here is when Bagent commits to the throw. Burden is still working through his break when Bagent begins his throwing motion, so he’s throwing to where Burden is going to be rather than waiting for him to fully uncover. There’s an underneath defender in the throwing lane and a deeper defender closing from behind, making the timing and placement important.

Bagent clears the underneath defender’s reach and gets the ball to Burden before the deeper defender can close the window. I’d still like him to locate it a little better and let Burden keep his cleats on the grass, but I’m not docking him for having to leave his feet here. Burden secures the ball and finishes the catch through contact, giving the Bears a 20-yard gain created primarily through the air.

In all honesty, Good feels right here. The anticipation and intermediate accuracy work together to produce an explosive completion on first down, without needing Burden to manufacture the yardage after the catch. This was something that Bagent sorely missed in his 2023 tape, so it’s great to see it come to light almost immediately against the Jets.

Situation: 1st Quarter, 2nd and 8 CHI45 06:18
Play Grade: Great
Result: 22-yard completion to Luther Burden III
Notes: (+) Anticipation (+) Explosive Play (++) Mid-Level Accuracy/Completion

Analysis: This is a great example of Bagent throwing with anticipation and backing it up with excellent placement. The Bears pair Burden’s deep over route from the top of the screen with Odunze’s backside post creating a deep Scissors concept which threatens the deep middle of the field.

What I really like here is that Bagent trusts where Burden is going. He commits to the throw while the trailing defender is still close, putting the ball into the space Burden is working toward instead of waiting for a more obvious window.

The accuracy is what really elevates this play. Bagent puts the ball out in front along Burden’s crossing path, giving him a chance to secure it while keeping it beyond the trailing defender’s reach. That defender is close enough for the placement to matter, and Bagent delivers exactly where he needs to, which also allows Burden to make a play after the catch and pick up some YAC to boot.

Situation: 2nd Quarter, 1st and 10 CHI43 11:52
Play Grade: Poor, Turnover Worthy
Result: Pass Intercepted by Minkah Fitzpatrick
Notes: (–) Late Throw (–) Ball Placement/Accuracy (–) Throw Leading to Turnover

Analysis: This is a poor throw from Bagent that turns into a turnover. Loveland runs the deep dig from the bottom of the screen, with Kmet working a shorter inside route underneath and a vertical route from Odunze on the opposite side stretching the coverage. Loveland initially has some room as he turns inside, but that window doesn’t stay open.

The ball needs to arrive as Loveland comes out of his break. Instead, the late timing on the throw gives Fitzpatrick a chance to close from depth and work back into the play. By the time the pass reaches Loveland, Fitzpatrick has erased the separation and is moving across his path.

The placement compounds that problem. Bagent needs to lead Loveland across the field and keep the ball away from the closing defender. Instead, he puts it into Fitzpatrick’s path, allowing him to cross in front of Loveland and take the interception. Loveland ends up trying to reach through the defender to get to the ball.

What makes this turnover worthy is that the timing and location give the defense the advantage at the catch point. Fitzpatrick deserves credit for closing and finishing the play, but Bagent’s throw and hesitation to throw gives him that opportunity. The late delivery makes the window harder to hit, the placement favors the defender, and the result is a turnover.

Situation: 2nd Quarter, 3rd and 5 CHI47 00:27
Play Grade: Elite
Result: 37-yard Completion to Rome Odunze
Notes: (+) Explosive Play (+) Touch/Layering (+) Anticipation (++) Deep-Level Accuracy/Completion

Analysis: This is an elite throw from Bagent, with the anticipation, touch, and accuracy all showing up together. At the top of the screen, the Bears run a variation of Mills, pairing Odunze’s post with Burden’s dig underneath and Raymond working out to the flat. The dig threatens the space underneath the safety, while Rome’s post attacks behind him.

What I really like is that Bagent commits to the throw before Rome has created obvious separation. The defender is still close as Odunze breaks inside, but Bagent trusts the route and throws into the space he’s working toward. He lets the separation develop while the ball is traveling instead of waiting for Rome to look completely open, which again was something Bagent really struggled with in 2023, so this just further goes to show the development of the young QB.

The touch and placement are excellent. Bagent gives the ball enough height to clear the underneath coverage, then brings it down ahead of Odunze and away from the trailing defender. He finds the space between those defenders without hanging the pass up and giving them time to recover.

Rome reaches up to secure it, comes down running, and turns the completion into a 37-yard gain. He deserves credit for the yards after the catch, but Bagent’s placement gives him that opportunity. On third down with less than thirty seconds left in the half, that’s a huge play, setting up an opportunity for points heading into the half.

Situation: 3rd Quarter, 1st and 10 CHI20 0:57
Play Grade: Above Average
Result: 14-yard Completion to Luther Burden III
Notes: (+) Anticipation, (+) Mid-Level Accuracy/Completion

Analysis: Bagent picks up fourteen yards here by anticipating Burden’s adjustment and putting the ball into the space the coverage gives him. Burden pushes vertically from the bottom of the screen, with Kmet working toward the sideline underneath. A defender stays over the top while another runs closely with Burden, leaving room to bring the throw back underneath.

Bagent starts his delivery before Burden turns to meet the pass. It looks like a back-shoulder adjustment to the vertical route, and the timing matters. Waiting for Burden to turn around would give the nearby defender more time to recognize the throw and close on the catch point.

The ball gives Burden a chance to secure it before that defender can get through him. Burden has to adjust and goes down making the catch, so the placement doesn’t earn extra credit, but Bagent delivers a catchable pass in the available window and moves the chains. Just another example of the strides Bagent has taken as a passer since 2023.

Summary

Bagent finishes Week 4 with final grades of 1st Half (-2.35) / 2nd Half (0.50) / Game (-1.85), landing in the lower half of my “Average” range against the Jets.

This was definitely a tale of two halves for Bagent. All three of his turnover-worthy plays came before halftime, along with the majority of his negatively graded throws, dragging what was otherwise a fairly efficient afternoon down considerably. The second half was much cleaner. Bagent didn’t record a single turnover-worthy, Poor or Bad graded play after halftime, finishing that portion of the game with a positive 0.50 grade.

That’s probably the best way to summarize how I came away feeling about the performance as a whole.

There were still some of the limitations we’ve seen from Bagent in the past, particularly when pressure forced him off schedule, and three turnover-worthy throws in one half simply can’t be ignored. At the same time, I thought there were legitimate signs of growth from the quarterback I graded back in 2023. He operated the offense more comfortably, generally kept Chicago on schedule and, once he settled down, avoided compounding mistakes while the Bears completely took control of the game around him.

Of the quarterbacks I’m grading this season, you can see where Bagent’s Week 4 score landed him 5th of 5 players graded in Week 4. For a look at the entire season thus far, along with some quick notes on the other quarterbacks from this week, you can find that here.

And unlike the last couple of weeks, there isn’t much mystery about who I’ll be grading next.

Ben Johnson has already announced that Bagent will get another start Sunday at Lambeau Field against the Packers while Caleb Williams continues working his way back from the hamstring injury he suffered in Week 2. Johnson called Bagent “the guy” for Week 5, meaning he’ll now get something neither Keenum nor Bagent had over the previous two weeks: a second consecutive start and another full week of preparation knowing the offense is his.

That’s going to make next week’s evaluation particularly interesting.

Sunday showed us some real improvement from the player we last saw starting games in 2023, but it also showed there are still areas where his limitations can put the football in danger. Now he’ll take that into Lambeau Field for a divisional matchup where the Bears probably won’t be able to survive three turnover-worthy throws in a half.

We’ll see which version of Bagent shows up.

Until then, Bear Down!

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

Here we go.

The smoke began to circulate last night when former Broncos wide receiver and now radio personality Brandon Stokley tweeted out that he is hearing that “Sean Payton is going to be taking over play calling this week”. Then, this morning, Pro Football Talk’s Mike Florio is also reporting that Payton will be calling plays on Sunday, not Davis Webb.

Well now, the national reporters have picked up this story, and it appears to be true. According to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo, Denver Broncos Head Coach Sean Payton will be more heavily involved in the offensive play-calling this week.

Rapoport adds that the process will remain collaborative, with offensive coordinator Davis Webb continuing to be a major voice on game days, but Payton will have a larger say in the process.

Payton met with the media on Wednesday and was asked if a four-game sample size was enough to evaluate a play caller. He told reporters that “our focus needs to be more on the specifics and the detail of each play regardless,” but did add, “certainly this isn’t championship football”.

“I think our focus needs to be more on the specifics and the detail of each play regardless. I think [Offensive Coordinator] Davis [Webb] is very fast and quick and understands what we’re doing. So I appreciate the question, but I think that the most important job I have is really evaluating the why’s. I think collectively we all after a game… After a four-game sample size… All right, certainly this isn’t championship football or what we see, how quickly can we correct those things?”

This switch had to happen, and it makes sense for Payton to take the reins once again. Let’s face it, the offense has been bad. Every part of the offense has taken a step back from last season. Nix has been inconsistent and hasn’t looked like the quarterback we saw vs. the Bills last season. The run game is nonexistent again, and JK Dobbins is either hurt or washed. Courtland Sutton went from being a 1,000-yard receiver catching nearly 10 touchdowns to having 9 catches for 86 yards and 0 touchdowns through 4 games. Remember Jaylen Waddle and how he was going to transform the offense? Well, now, outside of one game vs. the Jaguars, he has not been featured and feels like an afterthought in the offense.

The Broncos could not afford to let this Davis Webb play-calling experiment continue much longer with these results. They are likely in a short Super Bowl window right now and are off to a poor start. They need to make changes, get things rolling again, and look like the offense that clicked against the Packers and Bills late last season.

They play the 0-4 Chargers this Sunday, who are banged up and struggling on all sides of the ball. They cannot afford to struggle or lose against this team, with the Seahawks coming to town on a short week next Thursday. Hopefully, this move gets the offense rolling in the right direction, and we see a better offensive output moving forward,

item.title: Sean Payton to reportedly take an increased role in offense after team's slow start under Davis Webb
item.description: The Broncos have struggled on offense to open the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos opened the 2026 NFL season as Super Bowl contenders thanks to a dominant defense and an offense on a verge of a breakout thanks to third-year quarterback Bo Nix.

Through four games, neither side of the ball has held up its end of the bargain. The team's defense has allowed at least 24 points in three of its four games, though those have come against tough opponents.

The more concerning aspect of the team is its offense, which ranks 27th in points scored and has seen a massive decline in the run game and a lack of progression from Nix.

Because of that, head coach Sean Payton will play a larger role in the team's offense starting in Week 5, per ESPN.

The Broncos are taking a more collaborative play-calling approach this week with HC Sean Payton having an increased role in the process and OC Davis Webb continuing with a significant game-planning and game-day role, per sources. Denver is looking to spark its offense ahead of… pic.twitter.com/6y2jHZTaYn

— Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 8, 2026

Based on that report, Payton will be more involved in the process, but offensive coordinator Davis Webb will continue with his usual "game-day role." Webb will also reportedly be involved heavily in the team's offensive game plan.

For years, Payton has been considered one of the top offensive minds in the game. He helped Drew Brees become a Hall of Fame player, nearly made the playoffs with Jameis Winston and Trevor Siemian under center, and got an excellent statistical year out of a declining Russell Wilson. Prior to 2026, Payton had calling offensive plays in every single season in which he was a head coach in the NFL.

But Webb's emergence resulted in Payton finally giving up those duties. Webb, who previously served as the team's offensive pass game coordinator and quarterbacks coach, received multiple interviews for head-coaching jobs during the offseason. He didn't get any of those jobs, and was promoted to the Broncos' offensive coordinator after Joe Lombardi was fired. Given the amount of interest in Webb over the offseason, the team may have allowed him to take over as the offensive play caller as a way to make him happy and keep him around longer.

But that experiment hasn't gone well through four games. After leading the NFL in passing attempts last year, Nix is once again getting a ton of work to open the season. But the quarterback has taken a step back early and has put up career-low numbers in various statistical categories through four games — including completion percentage, yards per game, success rate and touchdown rate.

Despite Nix's struggles, the team hasn't adapted its play style. The Broncos have attempted just 90 rushing attempts through four weeks, which ranks tied for 29th in the NFL.

In Webb's and Nix's defense, the Broncos have played a murderer's row of defenses to open the year. All of the team's first four opponents rank within the top 10 in points against so far. Better things are almost certainly on the horizon for Denver no matter who calls plays moving forward.

Sure enough, the Broncos have a much easier task — on paper, at least — in Week 5. They'll take on the 0-4 Los Angeles Chargers, which have the 24th-ranked defense in the NFL heading into the contest.

item.title: NFL Secret Superstars, Week 4: Kyle Monangai, Alim McNeill, and Banana the Corgi are NFC standouts
item.description: Ben Johnson rode Kyle Monangai to an old-school win, Alim McNeill was a rare bright spot in Detroit’s defense, and Banana the corgi ran the perfect post route.
item.content:encoded:
Superstars may lead the discussion when it comes to success in the NFL, but more often than not, it’s the guys you barely know who will make the plays needed when they’re needed. Such players can be underrated for all kinds of reasons. Perhaps they’re playing in a smaller market, and the media isn’t appropriately trumpeting their exploits. Maybe they’re hidden in a depth chart behind bigger names who may not be doing as much. Or, it’s always possible that a wayward coach hasn’t quite figured out that one guy needs elevation to bring better results to the team.

Whatever the reason, we at SB Nation always like to bring the underrated names to you with the offseason Hidden Gems and in-season Secret Superstars series. You can also catch up on the AFC and NFC Secret Superstars for the 2026 season right here.

Here are our NFC Secret Superstars for Week 4 of the 2026 regular season. And if you haven’t yet, download the new SB Nation app, so you can better read our stuff and join the conversation wherever you are!

Kyle Monangai, RB, Chicago Bears

One thing you have to love about Chicago Bears head coach and offensive shot-caller Ben Johnson is that the man will win on that side of the ball in just about any way possible. Johnson’s passing game concepts are justifiably highly regarded, but going back to his time as the Detroit Lions’ offensive coordinator from 2022-2024, Johnson has also put some great run concepts on the field.

This approach really showed up in Chicago’s 23-12 win over the New York Jets on Sunday. With Tyson Bagent as his quarterback, Johnson wanted to keep the ball as much as possible, which led to a decidedly old-school approach. The Bears ran the ball 54 times for 232 yards and two touchdowns. Those 54 attempts tied for the fifth-most by one team in a single game in the new millennium. The Bears had more first downs (34) than the Jets had offensive plays (32), and the time of possession — 42:45 to 17:15 in the Bears’ favor — told you all you needed to know about Johnson’s strategy.

“It’s one of those things, as a play caller, you just kind of get in the flow of what do you think’s going to help us move the ball,” Johnson said postgame. “I’m always hungry and hunting big plays, explosive plays. Sometimes they’re there, sometimes they’re not. But I didn’t feel a whole lot of negative plays today, which was kind of indicative of us being able to possess the ball. I don’t know if we had the ‘super explosives’ like we would have wanted, either. But I know there weren’t a whole lot of third downs, or at least third and longs that I had to dial up there. It was just interesting how that all played out.”

Key among Johnson’s prime movers was Kyle Monangai, the second-year seventh-round man from Rutgers who has been a Secret Superstar before — back in Week 1, as a matter of fact — but I had to get him back in here after his game against the Jets. The 5’9”, 209-pound Monangai ran the ball 30 times for 146 yards and two touchdowns. He had an EPA per rush of +0.12, a rushing success rate of 46.7%, and he had just one negative run on those 30 attempts.

“He ran hard, yeah, he ran really hard,” Johnson said of his primary back. “He found some creases and turned on the gas. I thought I saw one really, really good stiff arm there as well. When you see a guy running like that, you want to feed him as the play caller. And I do think it elevates all of those guys out there and gives them a spark as well — the guys blocking for him. And it was good to see. We needed that.”

No matter how Monangai did it, he did it well. He had 11 attempts with man blocking for 53 yards and one touchdown, and 19 attempts with zone blocking for 93 yards and another score. Monangai has already proven the ability to be a rotational star, but in this game, he was the bell cow back, and he handled that responsibility like a champ.

Alim McNeill, DL, Detroit Lions

If you’ve watched the Detroit Lions’ defense this season, you don’t need me to tell you that it’s been a real big problem. These Lions are desperately scrambling to put a secondary on the field every week, and that’s a primary reason that only the Dallas Cowboys have a worse Defensive DVOA. All head coach Dan Campbell and defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard can do is sigh their way through it, as these Lions don’t have the linebackers to play zone the right way, and they don’t have the defensive backs to play man the right way.

Sadly, there isn’t really a third kind of defense that would help. In the Lions’ 32-26 Sunday night loss to the Carolina Panthers, Bryce Young riddled that defense with basic RPO stuff, and nobody seemed to know how to stop it.

The one guy who was a stopper to the extent the Lions would like was defensive tackle Alim McNeill. The 6’2”, 315-pound McNeill had a sack, seven total pressures, a tackle for loss in the run game, and generally speaking, wherever he was on the line, the offensive lineman (or linemen) on the other side of the ball was not going to have a good rep.

All this one week after his two-sack, seven-pressure performance against the New York Jets. In that game, Sheppard had McNeill take a shot as a stand-up rusher, to positive effect.

“Just find[ing] different ways to get creative [and] generate a rush is all we’re doing right now,” Sheppard said last week of that strategy. “Finding guys, making sure we can put them in optimal position. You start to move around 54 [McNeill], 97 [Aidan Hutchinson] makes a couple people wary. You look at the first two weeks, especially in the Buffalo game, Josh Allen’s like, ‘Whoa, whoa, whoa.’ And he’s checking to max protection when [he doesn’t] even have to and things like that. Trying to dictate [and] force the offenses to believe we’re doing certain things and sell[ing] different things. It’s kind of a mixture of that, and to get our premium rush players in one-on-one rush situations.”

Well, when very few things work, it’s a good time to empty the whole damned playbook. Especially with a guy in Alim McNeill, who is holding the standard when few others are able.

Banana, Corgi Race Champion, Seattle Seahawks

There are times when an unexpected athletic performance, combined with a particularly sassy style, goes viral for all the right reasons.

This was the case at the half of the Seattle Seahawks’ 30-23 Sunday win over the Los Angeles Chargers. That’s because the Seahawks held corgi races at halftime (these should happen everywhere more often, as my esteemed colleague James Dator pointed out), and a five-year-old corgi named Banana stunted on every other corgi in the race. To the extent that, after discounting a slight early start by the dog in the middle lane, Banana was able to look back at her unfortunate competitors in Usain Bolt fashion, telling those other corgis that this was NOT going to be their day.

From a sheer tools/technique perspective, the way Banana was able to run with such speed up the seam, and then take the post route over the ostensible defender, was the way you want to run a post pattern. Even Jaxon Smith-Njigba could learn a thing or two about separation here. Then, the backward look, and an overjoyed bounce into the end zone.

Pure art.

As you might expect, this was not Banana’s first rodeo. As Sofia Schwarzwalder of the Seattle Times reports, Banana has won these races before, and represented her favorite team in the Pro Bowl, the NFC Championship game, and during Super Bowl week.

Anne Pham, Banana’s human, said that she started racing Banana in 2023 at Emerald Downs, the thoroughbred racetrack outside of Seattle. Banana unexpectedly won her heat, and a star was born. Banana has also thrown out the first pitch at a Seattle Mariners game, and she’s kind of a big deal on both TikTok and Instagram.

“I grew up always wanting a dog,” Pham said. “I had in my iPhone notes that I would get a dog, specifically a corgi, and I would name it Banana. She was always in the future plans.”

As Banana’s performance coach, Pham doesn’t have to do a lot of refinement work with such a natural athlete; the primary strategy in Sunday’s race was to have Banana’s favorite stuffed banana at the finish line.

Clearly, it worked like a charm. Pham and Banana, who recently moved from Seattle to New York City and flew back for this game, have inspired greatness in each other.

Long may it continue.

item.title: PFT's Week 5 2026 NFL picks
item.description: Our take on all 15 games to be played this weekend.
item.content:encoded:
I've got a problem when it comes to guessing who'll win the standalone games. Basically, I currently suck.

For the games that had the stage to themselves in Week 4, I was 0-4. Fortunately, I was otherwise 10-2. And a final result of 10-6 is better than the Week 3 mark of 8-8.

But every week is a clean slate. A new opportunity to turn 0-0 into something that isn't embarrassing.

For the year, I'm 37-27. Which is good, but far from great. At least it's not horrible, which is mainly what I'm trying to avoid.

The best pick for Week 4 was the 49ers over the Broncos. Worst pick: Lions over Panthers. Flew too close to the sun on wings of pastrami pick: Saints over Falcons.

My seat-of-the-pants prognostications for all 15 of the Week 5 appear below, one wild-ass guess at a time. (The Panthers and Chiefs are off, as the bye weeks begin.)

Buccaneers at Cowboys (Thursday night)

Could undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels make a big splash in prime time? Yes, especially if the Cowboys take the Buccaneers too lightly. Every Tampa loss has come in a one-score game. If the Bucs can withstand the early onslaught, they have a chance.

I'll lean toward the Cowboys not being caught napping, and the Bucs not being able to avoid slipping into an early hole against an offense that is still trying to live up to its self-applied nickname.

Cowboys 34, Buccaneers 13.

Eagles vs. Jaguars (London)

The Eagles went from 2-0 with plenty of questions to 2-2 with few answers. Given the injuries and the roster turmoil, it will take all of coach Nick Sirianni's abilities and then some to engineer a win after a flight to London. And it will require the Jaguars to regard the Eagles as an early bye week.

Jaguars 27, Eagles 12.

Bears at Packers

In any divisional game, anything can happen. But the Bears, even without starting quarterback Caleb Williams, have the better team. They also have a head coach who needs to back up his big talk about Chicago's top rival.

Bears 27, Packers 20.

Bengals at Dolphins

Miami simply isn't good enough, on either side of the ball. The Bengals, who have big aspirations, can't afford to lose their third in a row — especially in a game they absolutely should win.

Bengals 26, Dolphins 14.

Raiders at Patriots

Last year, the Raiders went to Gillette Stadium and gave the Patriots a dry shave with a rusty razor. The Patriots, who rediscovered their swagger at Buffalo, surely remember that. If they don't, coach Mike Vrabel will spend the entire week reminding them of it.

Patriots 27, Raiders 24.

Vikings at Saints

The Vikings' strong finish to 2025 has carried over. The Saints' strong finish to 2025 has not.

Vikings 23, Saints 17.

Browns at Jets

How good are the 2026 Browns? I didn't even think twice about this one.

Browns 17, Jets 10.

Colts at Steelers

Pittsburgh's schedule suddenly has plenty of winnable games on it. This week, the Steelers go three extra days to get ready, and the Colts had to fly back from London.

Steelers 24, Colts 20.

Texans at Titans

Not even The Weather Channel wants to televise this one. If the Texans can't finagle a win, their remaining games should land on public-access TV.

Texans 21, Titans 16.

Giants at Commanders

Jayden Daniels's return should give the Commanders a spark. As long as the brace he'll be wearing on his elbow works.

Commanders 27, Giants 23.

Broncos at Chargers

Sean Payton picked the right spot to get back into calling plays. Still, it's a sudden must-win game for a team that has much higher aspirations than just making it to the playoffs.

Broncos 27, Chargers 17.

Lions at Cardinals

Whether Dan Campbell likes it or not, the Lions are mediocre. Fortunately for Detroit, the Cardinals are less than mediocre.

Lions 24, Cardinals 23.

49ers at Seahawks

The Seahawks can't afford to fall two games behind the 49ers. And Seattle vividly remembers losing at home to San Francisco last year.

Seahawks 21, 49ers 17.

Ravens at Falcons (Sunday night)

A Ravens team without Lamar Jackson is no match for the prime-time Falcons.

Falcons 30, Ravens 21.

Bills at Rams (Monday night)

This potential Super Bowl preview won't be if the Rams can't start winning more consistently.

Rams 38, Bills 35.

item.title: Pittsburgh Steelers WR Michael Pittman Jr. out multiple weeks
item.description: Steelers lose WR Michael Pittman for multiple games.
item.content:encoded:
It appears to be one step forward and one step back for the Pittsburgh Steelers in terms of injury news.

On Thursday, the team opened the activation window for safety DeShon Elliott, who began the season on IR. The Steelers will have 21 days to activate Elliott to the active roster. However, Pittsburgh will now be without another contributor for multiple games.

Wide receiver Michael Pittman was spotted in the locker room using a scooter to keep his inured foot elevated. Head coach Mike McCarthy says the injury will keep Pittman out multiple weeks.

“It’s gonna be a multiple-week injury,” McCarthy said via Chris Adamski.

Pittman was acquired from the Indianapolis Colts in a trade that involved a Day Three pick swap. To say his first month as a Steeler was been underwhelming would be an understatement, as he has caught just seven passes for 89 yards.

item.title: Kelvin Sheppard: Lions S Brian Branch looks ready to play now
item.description: Is there an outside chance Brian Branch plays this week vs. the Cardinals? Apparently he looks ready.
item.content:encoded:
After watching Brian Branch practice just one time following his 10 month rehab from an Achilles tear, Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard couldn’t hold in his excitement.

“How many positions can he play and how fast?” Sheppard joked with the media on Thursday.

And while that was a joke, Sheppard insisted that Detroit’s Pro Bowl safety looked so locked in and ready on Wednesday that he believes Branch could play a game on Thursday, if cleared.

“If we were playing tonight, it would be realistic,” Sheppard said. “Like, this dude—it’s like he hadn’t been out. I’m serious. It literally looks like he hasn’t been out. It’s unbelievable. So, it’s just a matter of I’m going to lean on (Director of Player Health) Brett Fisher, (Head Trainer) Mike Sundeen, and our medical staff here. They’ve always done a tremendous job, and whatever they tell me. If that’s 20 plays, if that’s 30, if it’s 50—I want it to be 60—but whatever they tell me, I’m going to lock that, and we’re going to roll.”

It would be pretty unorthodox for the Lions to put Branch into the starting lineup after just three practices, since he hasn’t been on the field since early December. And even Sheppard admitted they need to make sure they don’t put Branch in a tough position.

“We also gotta do right by that player,” Sheppard said. “So just make sure we pick and choose how much, how soon, where, what’s best for him right now, and just kinda take that approach to him.”

The Lions have taken a somewhat conservative approach with Branch throughout his rehab, ensuring that he was fully ready before they even put him back on the practice field. While Branch has been eager to get out there, he said Wednesday that he appreciates them keeping both his short and long-term health in mind. That said, he feels like only a few things stand between him and playing time on Sundays.

“Just catching my wind. That’s the only hurdle, I feel like,” Branch said. “Catching my wind and contact with each other. Just getting more contact with each other. Yeah, more one-on-ones.”

When Branch is back, he can have a significant impact on the Lions’ bottom-ranked defense. Not only will his presence help out a safety group that has struggled through four weeks, but Detroit believes his playmaking and discipline can have a trickle down effect.

“He’s an instinctive, aware player and he’s a violent player,” coach Dan Campbell said this week. “And so, he’s got a knack for the football and his production, even if it’s not what it was in the immediate as he grows back to that will have an impact, I believe. And then with that, then it helps the guys around him. It makes the guys next to him better because this guy will be where he’s supposed to be. He’ll be able to make some plays and alleviate a little stress and whether it’s the other safety, the corner, Jack (Campbell), some of those things.”

It still seems like a long shot that the Lions would opt to play Branch on Sunday against the Cardinals, but it’s clear that Sheppard wants him as soon as possible.

“I’m ready for him to go all 70-80 (snaps). However many we play. Saints game, that was 90? Let’s go 90, BB. As much of Brian Branch as I can get right now, I want it.”

item.title: The Eagles keep punting on the field. Are they now punting on the 2026 season?
item.description: The Eagles had high hopes entering the season, but things are already going sideways in Philadelphia.
item.content:encoded:
Every once in awhile, you come across a statistic so damning, so indicative of a deeper problem that it glows. For the Philadelphia Eagles, that statistic is this: zero-for-12. That’s the Eagles’ third-down conversion rate last weekend in their collapse against the Rams. 

Zero-for-12. Third-and-1, third-and-2, third-and-anything … the Eagles had 12 opportunities to keep drives alive in what would have been a defining win against Los Angeles, and fell short 12 times.

You know what usually happens when you can’t get it done on third down, of course: You punt. 

In the days after the Rams collapse, the Eagles saw two significant personnel developments that made observers wonder if the punting kept on going after the game was done. On Tuesday, Lane Johnson, the 14-year veteran right tackle and franchise mainstay, announced his retirement, effective immediately. Johnson’s departure means Philadelphia now has a major hole to fill on the line — not the situation you want to see when your team is already struggling offensively. 

But Johnson’s announcement was only the prelude to the week’s big news: On Wednesday, the Eagles dealt guard/center Cam Jurgens to the Ravens for a pair of draft picks. When you’re already facing significant struggles on that side of the ball, it’s tough to rationalize trading a Pro Bowler for draft picks as anything other than a concession until those draft picks suit up. 

If you’re taking a long view, the Eagles’ future looks bright. Philadelphia has four draft picks in the first two rounds of the 2028 draft thanks to the deals that sent Jurgens and A.J. Brown out of town. But those picks, who are currently toiling away in college, do exactly nothing for Philadelphia’s needs right now … if in fact that’s a primary concern for the Eagles. 

Eagles GM Howie Roseman pushed back on the idea that the Jurgens trade is a sign that the 2-2 Eagles are folding the tents on 2026. “We're trying to win this year,” he said Wednesday. “You want to have an extended run, and so my job is to look at how we can have sustained success for a long period of time, and you don't get many opportunities to get second-round picks in trades and get flexibility.”

Yes, roster flexibility is definitely something fans prize when you’re in the middle of a season and facing a depleted and winnable division. 

Between the two departures this week and the fact that Pro Bowler Landon Dickerson remains on injured reserve, the Eagles are in real trouble along the offensive line. That’s not a great sign for a team that’s struggling to mount consistent drives. When you’re not quite sure what you’ll get out of your marquee running back, and you’re still not sure if you have a good quarterback with bad tendencies or a bad quarterback with occasional highlights, well … that’s not the foundation for a successful season. 

The O-line square dance is a smokescreen for the Eagles’ deep and persistent playcalling questions. The Eagles go through offensive coordinators like a hungry tourist devouring a Geno’s cheesesteak, quickly and often messily. In the six years under head coach Nick Sirianni, the Eagles have had five OCs: Shane Steichen, Brian Johnson, Kellen Moore, Kevin Patullo and now Sean Mannion. 

The pattern here isn’t hard to determine: the OCs who guided Philadelphia to the Super Bowl, Steichen and Moore, have since moved on to head-coaching gigs of their own with Indianapolis and New Orleans, respectively. The OCs who haven’t been able to get Philadelphia a win in the postseason have since just moved on, period. 

All of which leads to the question of Sirianni’s role and fate in all this. Yes, he’s taken the Eagles to two Super Bowls and won one, which would seem to buy you a bit of grace. In many NFL cities, he’d have a guaranteed job for a decade. But this is Philly, where you’re only as good as last week’s result … and last week’s result was worse than bad, it was embarrassing. That’s a fast way to get the fans to turn on you, hard, and when that happens … it’s time to start pricing movers, regardless of whether they have to bubble-wrap a Super Bowl trophy. 

So far this season, Philadelphia has beaten Washington and Tennessee — two of the NFL’s not-quite-juggernauts — by a total of six points, and gotten their doors blown off by Chicago and a Medicare-eligible Case Keenum. Given the chance to reset their season, the Eagles coughed up a 10-point lead over Los Angeles in the game’s final four minutes. 

Now, Philadelphia heads overseas to play the London — sorry, Jacksonville Jaguars, followed by the Carolina Panthers and a run through all three other teams in the NFC East. That’s the definition of a statement stretch — one way or another, we’ll know who the Philadelphia Eagles are when they head into their Week 10 break. More importantly, we’ll know whether they’re worth paying attention to for the rest of 2026, or whether it’ll be time to start hoping for better days in 2027 and beyond.

item.title: Seahawks All-22 review: The good and bad from Seattle’s win over the LA Chargers
item.description: Seattle got back to winning, but the Chargers showed there's still plenty of work to do.
item.content:encoded:
After the Seattle Seahawks suffered their first loss of the season, they returned to Lumen Field needing to bounce back and, more importantly, avoid letting one setback turn into a losing streak.

On the other side was a Los Angeles Chargers team that had yet to win a game this season. This was, therefore, a game Seattle needed to take care of before heading into a much more difficult stretch of the schedule.

The Seahawks did exactly that. But while the result was positive, the performance left some warning signs, and that’s where the good and the bad of this win come into play.

The Good

Brian Fleury is getting legitimately creative

Brian Fleury’s creativity is starting to look like more than just an early-season impression. It is becoming a defining characteristic of this offense. Against the Chargers, Seattle once again found different ways to put its playmakers in favorable situations, whether by moving pieces around or using players outside of their more traditional roles.

One of the best examples was Rashid Shaheed being placed in the backfield to take advantage of his speed, something the team was missing after the injury to Jadarian Price. The WR finished the game with two carries for 33 yards, including a 28-yard TD. Excellent blocking on this toss run, allowing Shaheed to read the field like a returner and find the space for the TD.

Excellent screen design. Shaheed motions across the formation to keep him as an option, and the ball goes to Wilson, who gets good blocks (especially from Christian Haynes) and then breaks a tackle at the end for the TD.

Good OC play-calling is about keeping the defense guessing. From the same formation and motion, you can call different plays. The design is very similar to what happened on Wilson’s TD, but this time the ball goes to Barner on the screen, who gets good yardage.

Excellent game plan.

Excellent call. Three TEs — actually, one sixth OL and two TEs — and only one WR. Everything points toward a run. The Chargers are committed to it, leaving Tory Horton one-on-one. I believe Horton should have had two options: a slant against off coverage and a fade if the defender played press. Quick pass and TD.

Emanuel Wilson makes the most of his opportunity

Emanuel Wilson probably had the most complete game of his NFL career: 21 carries for 81 yards and a touchdown, plus three receptions for 39 yards and another touchdown. That’s 120 yards from scrimmage and two touchdowns on an afternoon when Seattle desperately needed production from its backfield.

With Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet unavailable, Wilson received a bigger opportunity and made the most of it. I don’t necessarily think he’s the ideal running back for an offense that wants to consistently attack horizontally and outside, but he found ways to produce within what the offense was asking him to do.

This is the kind of snap he needs to have more often. The intended gap on this run is the B-gap, but he recognizes the good block from Grey Zabel, makes the cut inside and gets a solid gain.

Here, he simply puts his head down and runs. He doesn’t look for other options, even though the blocks from Barner and Abe Lucas don’t appear to be developing. Maybe a cut into the A-gap would have been the better option.

Wilson even showed that he could contribute as a blocker…

BOOM!

Drake Thomas answers back

After a game that was below his usual standard against Washington, Drake Thomas showed up in a big way against the Chargers — and he did it immediately.

On the first play of the game, Thomas intercepted Justin Herbert, showing good route recognition and making a play that immediately put Seattle in a favorable position — only for Sam Darnold to throw an interception on the very next snap. Good job recognizing the play-action, dropping into coverage and coming down with a poor throw from the QB. If he doesn’t make the interception, Josh Jobe probably does.

On this play, he diagnoses all of the misdirection on the Chargers’ reverse immediately. He takes a stiff arm, but his quick diagnosis slows the play down just enough for his teammates to finish it. This is how Mike Macdonald’s defense works, as we’ve discussed before.

Drake Thomas isn’t a big linebacker. He tries to compensate for that with a ton of film study. You can frequently see his quick diagnosis on plays like this, anticipating what’s coming and waiting for the RB to make the tackle.

And just because he’s undersized doesn’t mean he can’t be physical. Look at this hit on the fullback. BOOM!

The pass rush finally showed up

Herbert was pressured on 55% of his dropbacks, while Seattle finished the game with four sacks — plus a fifth that was wiped out by a roughing the passer penalty. The Chargers’ offensive line had its issues and lost players during the game, so there is some context here, but Seattle did what it needed to do: it took advantage of the situation.

The pressure was consistent, and in the end, it was a pass-rush play that decided the game. Uchenna Nwosu forced the strip-sack on the Chargers’ final drive and ended Los Angeles’ comeback attempt. Excellent work by Julian Love cutting off the passing lane and forcing the QB to hold onto the ball for too long.

Byron Murphy standing up is inevitable. Excellent swipe to get to the QB on one of the quickest sacks of the season.

Ernest Jones, who led the team in tackles and also had an interception, got his sack here. I think he made an adjustment before the snap based on the Chargers’ formation, and this is where the execution comes into play. He appears to attack OL #69 to open up space for the stunt, so the RB ignores him and waits for the looper. Jones gets around the blocker and gets the sack.

Nick Emmanwori doing it with pure athleticism. He changes direction as the play flows into play-action, escapes the fullback’s block and gets the sack.

The Bad

The run defense is starting to show a crack

If there is one place where the Seahawks are still essentially a brick wall, it’s the middle of the defensive line. Running directly at Byron Murphy II, Leonard Williams and Jarran Reed remains an extremely difficult task.

The problem is that opponents are starting to find an alternative.

Washington already showed last week that outside runs could be a way to attack this defense. The Chargers followed the exact same path and found some success, finishing with 147 rushing yards on 32 carries, an average of 4.6 yards per carry. They did it while producing runs of 26, 20, 15 and 9 yards.

The Seahawks need to defend the bubble on the left side of the defense — the open space between the gaps that the offense can attack when no defender immediately fills it. Byron Murphy absorbs the double team, but Nick Emmanwori plays too passively and doesn’t attack the fullback creating space for the running back.

Again, attacking the same space. Rylie Mills is moved by the double team, creating space and getting driven into Ernest Jones, which creates a lane for the run. Demarcus Lawrence not identified the run and also help to create the space for the offense.

Seattle needs to find an answer before this becomes an even bigger trend.

The offensive line is still searching for consistency

Seattle ran for 138 yards, a significant improvement from the 44 yards against Washington, but there is still a feeling that the running game isn’t producing consistently.

The situation doesn’t help. Seattle is without its top backfield options and has to work with a combination of Emanuel Wilson and George Holani. Wilson doesn’t appear to be the best fit for outside zone/wide zone, while Holani has struggled to create yards after contact.

The OL, including Abe Lucas and Grey Zabel, who both had a down game against the Commanders, took a step in the right direction. Even so, there were still some execution issues.

Lucas takes a poor angle from the beginning of the contact, losing the inside and forcing the RB to cut outside, preventing the play from succeeding.

On this play, Beau Stephens gets driven backward, once again forcing the RB to stretch the play horizontally and destroying the run.

Sam Darnold has a down game

Sam Darnold had a very different game from the one he played against Washington. The previous week, even while making some mistakes, he threw for 379 yards and four touchdowns and kept Seattle alive in a game where the running game provided almost no help.

Against the Chargers, his performance dropped significantly: 13-of-22 for 168 yards, two touchdowns and one interception, along with several other poor throws.

The interception was completely bizarre. There was absolutely no reason to force this throw, especially when it killed the momentum immediately after our defense had just intercepted Herbert.

Here, he escapes the pressure well, but the throw is terrible. Kupp has plenty of space in front of him, but the pass is behind him and is almost intercepted.

On this play, he takes too long to make a decision and read the defense. The George Holani’s protection isn’t good, but the play call puts the CB in conflict. He can’t cover both Shaheed and JSN, and there is a window for the throw. Darnold hesitates, gets the ball out a little too late, the pressure arrives, and the play ends up being much closer to an interception than a completion.

Third down has become a problem

This may be one of the biggest areas where Brian Fleury needs to find a solution.

Seattle converted just three of 12 third downs against the Chargers, a 25% conversion rate. And this problem didn’t start in this game. Against New England, they converted two of 11. Against Arizona, six of 13. Against Washington, three of nine.

In other words, excluding the dominant game against the Cardinals, Seattle has converted just five of 32 third downs in the other three games — a 15.6% conversion rate.

Defenses have been sending pressure without much concern, and the play calls haven’t been good enough. Obviously, the running game needs to exist first to avoid long third downs, but the play-calling and QB play can still improve.

The Chargers clearly bring a heavy blitz here, leaving the three receivers in man coverage. Mathematically, the Seahawks were going to have to leave at least one rusher unblocked.

The receivers don’t get immediate separation, and the route concept is somewhat confusing and takes too long to develop in this situation. It’s a bad call, but I also think Darnold could have made adjustments before the snap after recognizing the Chargers’ defensive alignment.

The previous week, Marcus Mariota escaped several situations because of exactly this.

The penalty avalanche nearly turned the win into a problem

If there is one thing that cannot be ignored from this game, it’s the lack of discipline. The Seahawks and Chargers combined for 30 penalties, the most in a single NFL game this season. Los Angeles had 16 penalties for 130 yards, while Seattle committed 14 penalties for 150 yards, a franchise record for penalty yardage.

And it wasn’t just about the volume. Some of those penalties had a direct impact on the scoreboard. Nick Emmanwori, who otherwise had an excellent individual game with nine tackles, two tackles for loss, one sack and two QB hits, committed an unnecessary roughness penalty on a third down that would have kept the clock running. Instead, Los Angeles got additional time and eventually kicked a field goal.

On the same afternoon, penalties by DeMarcus Lawrence and Hall involving contact with Herbert helped keep alive the drive that ended in a touchdown. In total, four of Seattle’s 15-yard penalties came during the Chargers’ two touchdown drives.

This is the kind of thing that has to disappear before the next few games. Against the Chargers, Seattle had enough of a cushion to survive its own mistakes. Against better opponents, giving a drive a second or third life can be the exact difference between a win and a loss.

It’s not a coincidence that a game Seattle led 27-6 ended with the Chargers having the ball and needing only one possession to tie it.

Final thoughts

It wasn’t the pretty win the Seahawks wanted. It was the win they needed.

Seattle was better than the Chargers in virtually every aspect of the game, but still allowed a team that entered the game with a 0-3 record to reach the final possession with a legitimate chance to tie the game — and potentially even take the lead with a successful two-point conversion.

The fumble on the final drive ended the threat and secured the win, but it also made it clear that there are problems that need to be fixed.

And that’s the most important point moving forward.

With an extremely difficult stretch of the schedule ahead, it’s much better to work through these problems after a win than to have to fix the same issues after a loss. The Seahawks got the result they needed. Now they need to make sure the same mistakes don’t show up again when the level of competition rises.

The win is here, now the work begins.

Go Hawks!

item.title: Are the Chiefs’ offseason bets on defense paying off 4 games in?
item.description: At 4-0, Kansas City’s offseason moves are paying off. Here’s how the additions and internal bets grade out.
item.content:encoded:
The offseason gave the Kansas City Chiefs fans plenty of reasons to ask what came next. Familiar faces departed, established defensive starters found new homes, and the Chiefs placed significant responsibility on players who had yet to take an NFL snap.

Four games later, the Chiefs enter their bye week at 4-0. That makes the changes easier to embrace, but an undefeated record does not automatically give every offseason decision an “A.”

The better question is whether Kansas City improved the roles it needed to improve through outside additions and the development of players already on the roster — and whether the early production supports the risks Brett Veach took.

We talked about the offensive changes yesterday. Let’s look on the defensive side:

Secondary: A major gamble is showing encouraging returns

Losing Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, and Bryan Cook in the same offseason raised legitimate concerns.

Kansas City responded with a combination of youth and experience: first-round cornerback Mansoor Delane, veteran safety Alohi Gilman, and the return of L’Jarius Sneed, alongside second-year cornerback Nohl Williams taking on a larger role.

Delane has provided the most compelling early evidence. The sixth-overall pick intercepted Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix in the opener and has recorded 20 combined tackles and three passes defended across three appearances. His shoulder injury interrupted that debut and cost him the game against the Indianapolis Colts, making his availability part of the evaluation.

His willingness to tackle is particularly encouraging. Delane recorded 10 combined tackles in each game against the Miami Dolphins and the Las Vegas Raiders. Our own Nate Christensen’s film review against the Raiders highlighted his ability to set the edge and prevent explosive runs, adding value beyond his coverage assignments.

Williams belongs in that evaluation, too. Kansas City’s plan depended in part on developing a cornerback already in the building. Through four games, he has recorded 15 combined tackles, four passes defended and a sack. Those contributions deserve attention when grading how the Chiefs handled the departures of McDuffie and Watson. The offseason bet was to trust the previous year’s investment to take another step.

Gilman, meanwhile, has recorded 17 combined tackles and a pass defended through four games. With Chamarri Conner making his season debut against Las Vegas, the safety rotation is still taking shape.

There is enough here to feel better about the transition. There isn’t enough to declare that the Chiefs have fully replaced everything McDuffie, Watson, and Cook provided.

Early grade: B

Defensive front: Promising pieces, unfinished work

The departures of Charles Omenihu, Mike Danna, Derrick Nnadi and Leo Chenal removed experience from several different defensive roles. Kansas City addressed the front by adding Khyiris Tonga and drafting Peter Woods and R Mason Thomas.

Those moves should be evaluated together without pretending they were direct, player-for-player replacements. Chenal’s departure also put the spotlight on an in-house option: Jack Cochrane. Kansas City re-signed Cochrane in March, and he was listed as a defensive starter against Las Vegas alongside Nick Bolton and Drue Tranquill. His place in the lineup illustrates another part of the offseason plan: retaining a familiar player and trusting him at linebacker. That decision deserves its own evaluation as the season continues, including how the group handles the defensive and special-teams responsibilities Chenal left behind.

Woods has recorded nine combined tackles and a pass defended through four games. Thomas has four combined tackles and one sack, which came in the season opener.

Those totals do not justify calling either player a finished product. They also don’t tell the whole story.

Against the Raiders, Thomas was credited with eight pressures, including five in the fourth quarter. That is meaningful evidence of disruption even though Thomas did not finish with a sack.

The next step is turning those opportunities into more drive-changing plays. Woods must continue developing his influence inside, while Thomas needs to make his pressure production repeatable.

The investment makes sense. The early results offer reasons for optimism, but this group still has more to prove than the backfield.

Early grade: C+

An encouraging start, with more to prove

My overall early offseason grade is a B+.

Walker remains my pick for the biggest addition, while finding a solid contributor at left tackle in undrafted rookie Benson represents another significant offseason win. Delane and Williams have provided encouraging returns at cornerback, and Thomas has shown why the Chiefs invested in his pass-rushing ability.

On the departure side, Washington Commanders linebacker Leo Chenal is the player I believe Kansas City misses most, particularly in its base defense and on special teams. That’s why the overall grade remains a B+: the Chiefs have made meaningful upgrades, but some of the roles left behind still need convincing answers. The remaining questions involve consistency, availability and whether the depth can handle a larger workload.

The McDuffie trade also deserves patience. Kansas City received four draft picks, including the No. 29 selection used on Woods and a 2027 third-rounder. You can’t settle its full value after four games.

For now, the Chiefs have won while introducing substantial change. The next stretch will reveal how much of that success their newcomers can sustain—and whether an encouraging offseason becomes the foundation for another postseason run.

item.title: Cowboys vs Buccaneers: 2 players Dallas should use more in Week 5
item.description: The Cowboys have a chance to build their first winning streak of the season.
item.content:encoded:
After a gut-check win over the Houston Texans last Sunday, the Dallas Cowboys face a short week as they prepare to host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Thursday night. While Tampa Bay does come into this game winless at 0-4, history has shown us that short weeks in the NFL make anything possible.

If the Cowboys want to win their second in a row, they’ll need to mix some things up. With that thought in mind, here are two players Dallas should use more on Thursday night.

1) EDGE Malachi Lawrence

Four games into the season, the Cowboys’ pass rush group has been very disappointing. Dallas is tied for the second-fewest sacks in the league with four, and has only two players, Rashan Gary and Quinnen Williams, with nine or more pressures on the year. 

Coming into the year, there was plenty of concern about the lack of quality pass-rushers on Dallas’ roster. While the Cowboys traded for Rashan Gary to raise the floor of their pass-rush group, they chose to bet on first-round pick Malachi Lawrence to make an immediate impact rather than acquiring another proven commodity to start alongside him.

So far, Lawrence has not been given a fair shot to do so. The 23-year-old has logged just 42 pass-rush snaps in Dallas’ first four games of the season. In those limited opportunities, Lawrence has flashed some big-time potential. The first-round pick has a 20.5 Pass-Rush Win%, the highest of any defender on the Cowboys’ roster, to go with five total pressures and four hurries.

While these numbers don’t jump off the page, it’s clear Lawrence has the tools to be an impactful pass rusher, and he should be given more opportunities to do so. This week against the Buccaneers, the Cowboys should increase Lawrence’s snap count and see if he can make more of an impact.

2) DT Otito Ogbonnia

The Cowboys made a few notable moves this offseason. At the time, signing defensive tackle Otito Ogbonnia didn’t seem like that significant of a move, but four games into the 2026 campaign, the veteran has been far and away their best defender against the run.

Four games in, Ogbonnia leads all Cowboys’ defensive linemen with 10 defensive stops and a 74.2 Pro Football Focus run defense grade. 

Despite being their best run defender, Ogbonnia has had two games this season (Washington/Houston) where he played 12 or fewer run-defense snaps. However they want to manage the rotation to rectify this, the Cowboys need to give Ogbonnia plenty of opportunities this week.

item.title: NFL Picks Week 5: Celebrating the Past
item.description: The first quarter of the 2026 NFL season has concluded and now we move forward with Week 5. What will this week have in store? Let’s take a look!
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints remain at home to face the Minnesota Vikings, to continue their disappointing season so far. After getting completely embarrassed by Atlanta last Monday Night, the Saints hope to stop the hemorrhaging against the undefeated Vikings. Despite not being a division rival, Minnesota may be the next most hated team for many Saints fans outside of the NFC South. Following the Falcons march through the city, New Orleans simply doesn’t need the Vikings to do the same.

Once again, the Saints will celebrate the past in the midst of lamenting the present. Drew Brees, who will be in the booth to call the game, will also be honored at halftime, the Hall of Famer’s second-consecutive game in attendance. The fans will have another opportunity to honor what came before, while wishing those times never had to pass. The Saints as an organization desperately needs to find a way to keep the fans and the region invested in the current-day franchise without leaning on days long past. That opportunity starts now, with another hated team coming into New Orleans. Win, and the chance to reinvigorate the fanbase grows larger. Lose, and the chance to lose the fanbase grows larger as well.

Let’s take a look at this and every matchup in Week 5.

Last week I went 9-7

I told you so: Panthers over Lions!

What do I know: Saints over Falcons?

***

WEEK 5

Thursday, October 8th – Thursday Night Football

Buccaneers(0-4) at Cowboys(2-2)

Dallas’ roller coaster season will finally give them a break against the beleaguered Bucs. Dallas wins 35-20.

Pick: Cowboys

***

Sunday, October 11th – Very Early Game

Eagles(2-2) at* Jaguars(3-1) – London, England

This tight contest will come down to a late field goal by Philly on the final play. Philadelphia wins 27-25.

Pick: Eagles

***

Sunday, October 11th – Early Games

Bengals(2-2) at Dolphins(0-4)

Cincy gets themselves back on track against the lowly Dolphins in Miami. Cincinnati wins 35-17.

Pick: Bengals

***

Raiders(3-1) at Patriots(2-2)

This will be a tight contest throughout, but trailing by a point, Klint Kubiak schemes a touchdown to win the game in the closing moments. Las Vegas wins 23-17.

Pick: Raiders

***

Browns(3-1) at Jets(1-3)

This will be a far more entertaining game than the names attached to it would suggest. Cleveland wins 37-27.

Pick: Browns

***

Colts(2-2) at Steelers(2-2)

This is a surprisingly crucial game for both teams as they look to keep pace in their respective divisions. Indianapolis wins 24-20.

Pick: Colts

***

Texans(0-4) at Titans(0-4)

The Texans have not bottommed-out yet, until now, and heads might roll in Houston after this one. Tennessee wins 21-7.

Pick: Titans

***

Giants(3-1) at Commanders(1-3)

Jameis Winston will lead one of the NFL’s most improved teams to another win. New York wins 29-13.

Pick: Giants

***

Bears(3-1) at Packers(2-2)

At this point, Ben Johnson could suit up a 46-year-old Rex Grossman at QB and still lead Chicago to another routine victory. Chicago wins 27-16.

Pick: Bears

***

Vikings(4-0) at Saints(1-3)

No defense in the NFL has given up fewer points than the Minnesota Vikings squad, led by Brian Flores. Conversely, no defense in the NFL has given up more points than the New Orleans Saints squad, led by Brandon Staley. One might see where this is a problem. It looks as though the Vikings will score quite a bit in this game, while the Saints won’t. It’s a shame honestly, considering where the Saints have fallen since their win in Baltimore in Week 2. Not just a fall in the standings, but the fall in confidence and faith of the fans. Despite it all, the Dome should be loud, even with the amount of purple that will be in attendance, but like the last two home games, there will simply be too many obstacles for Kellen Moore’s team to overcome. Minnesota wins 31-19.

Pick: Vikings

***

Sunday, October 11th – Late Games

Broncos(2-2) at Chargers(0-4)

Denver rebounds from last week’s loss, with a dominant win over the sad-sack Chargers in Los Angeles. Denver wins 21-7.

Pick: Broncos

***

Lions(2-2) at Cardinals(1-3)

Arizona is better than their record shows, and Detroit is worse, much worse. Arizona wins 14-10.

Pick: Cardinals

***

49ers(4-0) at Seahawks(3-1)

These bitter NFC West rivals will show us all what a huge rivalry game is supposed to look like. This slugfest will go back and forth, but the Niners find a way to win on the road. San Francisco wins 20-13.

Pick: 49ers

***

Sunday Night Football

Ravens(3-1) at Falcons(2-2)

No Lamar Jackson? No chance against the red-hot Falcons in Atlanta. It’s just another dominant primetime win for the birds. Atlanta wins 34-21.

Pick: Falcons

***

Monday, October 12th – Monday Night Football

Bills(3-1) at Rams(2-2)– Game of the Week

This highly-anticipated Monday Night showdown should be infinitely more competitive and entertaining than last Monday Night’s debacle. Many consider this a Super Bowl preview, we’ll see about that, but even without those lofty expectations, this game will be phenomenal. It will be razor-close, but the home team finds a way to win in the end. Los Angeles wins 37-34.

Pick: Rams

***

There we go, Week 5 is shaping up to be pretty interesting. Leave us your picks, comments, and insight below!

item.title: Steelers WR Michael Pittman Jr. will miss multiple games after re-injuring his foot
item.description: Steelers wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr. won't play against his former team when the Colts come to town on Sunday, and he won't play for a while after that, either.
item.content:encoded:
Steelers wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr. won't play against his former team when the Colts come to town on Sunday, and he won't play for a while after that, either.

Pittsburgh head coach Mike McCarthy said today that Pittman will miss time after re-injuring his foot, and it's too soon to say whether he will have to go on injured reserve.

"It's the same foot, so it's going to be a multiple-week injury," McCarthy said. "We're still going through the evaluation of his roster position."

The Steelers traded for Pittman in March and signed him to a three-year, $59 million contract extension, but so far that hasn't looked like a great investment. Pittman has just seven catches for 89 yards this season.

A 2020 second-round pick of the Colts out of USC, Pittman had two 1,000-yard receiving seasons in Indianapolis and appeared to have a long and promising career ahead of him, but his production declined over the last couple seasons with the Colts, and now the Steelers' primary focus will be on getting him healthy.
